Name: The Roman Legion's Code of Marching Camps and the Discipline of Nightly Watchwords on Wooden Tablets
RagShortTexts: Every day on the march, a Roman legion had to build a standard square fortress within a few hours
Deep ditch, high rampart and palisade, two main roads crossing, with the commander's tent and the eagle standard at the center
Sentries in four watches passed on the watchword on wooden tablets; anyone who fell asleep or left his post was cudgeled to death
BaseText: The core secret of the Roman legions' ability to fight again and again without defeat on distant campaigns was their strictly standardized, mechanically precise procedure for building marching camps (Castrametation). At the end of each day's march, advance surveyors had already chosen high ground that was level, sheltered from the wind and near water. When tens of thousands of infantry arrived, half stood guard in armor while the other half put down their packs and, within two hours, dug a standard ring ditch three meters wide and three meters deep, piled the excavated earth into a thick earthen rampart, and planted it densely with the wooden stakes they carried to form a strong defensive line. The camp was strictly square or rectangular, with gates on all four sides, and inside, the cross-shaped main roads (Cardo and Decumanus) precisely divided the quarters of the infantry and cavalry, the headquarters and the altar of the standards. At night the whole camp kept watch in four shifts, and the watchword, inscribed on wooden tablets (Tessera), was checked and passed on from post to post. Any sentry who left his post, fell asleep or lost his tablet was cudgeled to death on the spot by his comrades under military law, with no pardon.

Variants.Content: Even when the enemy is still ten miles away, the shovel weighs as much as the javelin. Every night we build a small moving Rome on foreign soil, and whatever the wind and rain, our hearts are at peace.

The Romans are a pack of burrowing moles! We spied on them from the woods all day long, and the moment they stopped they threw up a ring of mud castle bristling with stakes. There was no way to get at them!

Once a Roman legion has built its camp, a battle of encirclement turns into a hopeless assault on a fortified position. General Hannibal lured the enemy out again and again precisely to destroy them on the march before they could build their camp.
